justice: The street has a wide paved carriageway and planted edges, but there is no clearly visible dedicated sidewalk, so space allocation is still car-oriented rather than balanced for all users.
Curbs run continuously along both sides of the road, yet no marked curb ramps or tactile paving are visible, limiting inclusive accessibility for diverse users.
The roadway appears smooth and unobstructed, which benefits general movement, but the lack of visible pedestrian crossings or designated cycle space reduces fairness across travel modes.
safety: Traffic volume appears very low, and the road is straight with clear forward visibility, which reduces immediate conflict risk for drivers and pedestrians.
There are no visible lane markings, crosswalks, or traffic-calming devices, so user priority is ambiguous and could create uncertainty if traffic increases.

Trees and landscape strips separate the road edge from adjacent open space and the building frontage, which provides some buffering, but the absence of a distinct pedestrian path weakens walking safety.
livability: The street edge includes trees, lawn, and shrubs, which improve environmental quality and make the setting more pleasant for everyday use.
A large open green field on the left provides a spacious visual environment, but there are no visible shops, seating areas, or active frontages that would support daily street life.
The building frontage appears mostly inactive at ground level, and the road feels like an access drive rather than a socially vibrant public street.
sustainability: Multiple street trees, planted lawns, and shrub beds contribute to urban greening and some ecological value.
The compact road width and apparently low traffic environment may help reduce transport intensity compared with a wider vehicular corridor.
No visible bike lane, bus stop, permeable paving, or stormwater features are present, so support for low-carbon mobility and water-sensitive design is only partial.
aesthetics: The landscaped roadside with evenly spaced trees and red shrubs creates a neat and visually coherent streetscape.
The asphalt surface and curbs appear newly maintained and clean, which contributes to a tidy appearance.
The open field on one side and modern building facade on the other create a simple, orderly composition, although the street lacks distinctive urban character.
comfort: Street trees provide some shade potential, but canopy cover is still limited and much of the road remains exposed to direct sun, reducing thermal comfort.
The asphalt surface is smooth and the corridor is free of clutter, which supports comfortable movement for general users.
No benches, shelters, or other resting amenities are visible along the route, which lowers physical comfort for people spending time outdoors.
The low-traffic setting and broad open space likely reduce noise and crowding, supporting psychological comfort.
walkability: No continuous, clearly designated sidewalk is visible on either side of the road, making pedestrian routes ambiguous.
Raised curbs define the road edge, but there are no visible crossings, curb ramps, or pedestrian markings to support safe route continuity.
The green landscaping and low traffic make the environment pleasant to walk through, yet the lack of pedestrian infrastructure keeps overall walkability modest.
bikeability: There is no visible bike lane, cycle track, or bicycle symbol marking, so cyclists would need to share the carriageway with motor vehicles.
The smooth asphalt surface and low apparent traffic volume are positive conditions for basic cycling comfort.
No bicycle parking, intersection treatments, or protective separation features are visible, which limits convenience and perceived cycling safety.
